newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil hikes land tax to speed agrarian reform.
newsitem.headline: Brazil hikes land tax to speed agrarian reform.

text.p: Brazil's Congress approved Wednesday a steep tax hike on unused farmland in an attempt to redress an acute concentration of land ownership and reduce often bloody conflict in the countryside.

"We have turned a dark page in Brazilian history," Agrarian Reform Minister Raul Jungmann said shortly after a joint session of Congress approved a presidential decree hiking the tax. "We are going to hit hard the non-productive sector which up until now has virtually never paid tax."

The new tax, which comes hard on the heels of two new laws aimed at speeding the government's land reform program, will levy a 20 percent charge on unused properties of more than 5,000 hectares and lower rates for smaller estates. Productive farms are not affected by the new law.

Of a total 331 million hectares of farmland in Brazil, about 150 million hectares lie unused, according to government figures. While the biggest private estate is roughly the size of Belgium, at least two million families need land, testimony to Brazil's failure over centuries to grapple with the distortions in land ownership in the country's remote regions.

Jungmann said the new tax would double the government's budget for settling landless farmers and force many landowners to sell their properties, mainly on the fringes of the Amazon region where they tend to be larger than in Brazil's more developed south.

The Amazon is also the region where most violence over land has arisen. Earlier this year, 19 landless farmers were killed in a clash with police as they demanded the right to settle an unused farm in the northern state of Para.

Earlier this month Congress approved two other bills considered crucial to speeding up Brazil's lagging land reform program. One sets down fixed time periods for the confiscation of unused land and its transfer to landless families. The other requires that public prosecutors accompany each stage of the process, reducing the likelihood of violence.

Brazil's Landless Movement, which encourages peasants to take over unused farmland, said the new tax, like the other measures, was an important step forward, but doubted it would be fully put into practice.
"Let's see if the government has the strength to actually implement this law. It certainly hasn't made landowners pay much tax up until now," said Neuri Rossetto, a director at the organization.
